title: Multivariate hyperdensity functional theory for inhomogeneous equilibrium fluids: From first principles to simulation-based machine learning
abstract: Hyperdensity functional theory facilitates the investigation of the equilibrium behavior of a general order parameter or statistical mechanical observable in spatially inhomogeneous classical many-body systems. The approach is based on applying the exact Mermin-Evans classical density functional mapping to an extended ensemble. Here we present the multivariate generalization for investigating simultaneously the properties and interrelations of several different hyperobservables of choice. The resulting framework gives rise to a systematic characterization and prediction scheme for general many-body phenomena. All pertinent equilibrium averages, variances, and covariances constitute universal density functionals, as we demonstrate explicitly. Associated one-body hyperfluctuation profiles quantify the degree of correlation of the local density with first- and second-order combinations of hyperobservables. These multivariate hyperfluctuation profiles are accessible in many-body simulations and they satisfy exact hyper-Ornstein-Zernike equations, which we derive from the minimization principle in the extended multivariate ensemble. The formal structure of the theory integrates naturally with supervised machine learning, which renders all hyperdensity functionals accessible in practice via training of neural networks on simulation data. We demonstrate all salient techniques using the illustrative case of clustering in confined hard rod fluids, thereby choosing the total number of particles and the largest cluster size as the representative hyperobservables of interest. Our numerical methodology enables the efficient and successful prediction of all statistical quantities induced by the chosen hyperobservables, which we verify via comparison to test data and which we attribute to the tight interplay of first-principles and machine-learning concepts that our general approach combines.
summary: This work presents a multivariate extension of hyperdensity functional theory to analyze multiple correlated observables in inhomogeneous fluids. It derives exact theoretical relationships, such as hyper-Ornstein-Zernike equations, governing the statistical interrelations between these observables. By coupling this rigorous theory with machine learning, the authors provide a powerful, systematic tool for predicting complex many-body behavior from simulation data.
main_problem: The paper develops a multivariate generalization of hyperdensity functional theory (HDFT) to systematically investigate the equilibrium properties and interrelations of multiple, arbitrary observables in inhomogeneous classical many-body systems.
main_result: The framework establishes universal density functionals for averages, variances, and covariances of these observables, and derives exact hyper-Ornstein-Zernike equations linking these correlation measures.
method: The theory is built upon extending the Mermin-Evans classical density functional mapping to an extended multivariate ensemble, and its practical implementation is achieved by integrating the functional structure with supervised machine learning via neural networks.
model_or_system: The theory is applied to classical many-body systems, illustrated specifically by studying the clustering behavior in confined hard rod fluids.
key_observables: Hyperobservables ($\{\hat{A}_\ell\}$), equilibrium averages, variances, covariances, and hyperfluctuation profiles ($\chi_{\hat{A}}(\mathbf{r})$).
important_parameters: Temperature (via $ eta$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and the coupling constants ($\lambda_\ell$) associated with the hyperobservables.
main_assumptions: The theory relies on the formal structure derived from the Mermin-Evans map, and practical calculation requires approximating the functionals using machine learning techniques.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the multivariate HDFT framework via the extended ensemble, derives the universal density functionals and the hyper-Ornstein-Zernike equations, and then details the mathematical machinery using functional derivatives (Gateaux derivatives) to compute these higher-order correlation functions, concluding with an application to hard rod fluid clustering.
why_interesting: While focused on classical fluids, the rigorous mathematical framework for calculating higher-order correlation functions and the explicit integration with machine learning for functional approximation are highly relevant methodologies for developing advanced theoretical tools in complex quantum many-body systems.
